newsitem.title: UK: Protestant leader hits out at N.Irish parade plan.
newsitem.headline: Protestant leader hits out at N.Irish parade plan.

text.p: Proposals for a powerful new commission intended to defuse sectarian tension surrounding Northern Ireland's annual parades were damned as a "protesters' charter" by a pro-British Protestant leader on Monday.

Jeffrey Donaldson, of the main Orange Order marching institution, said a report by a British-appointed study group had given the green light to Catholic nationalist protests that would worsen conflict surrounding Protestant marches during the traditionally turbulent summer "marching season"
Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring said with the marching season only months away, the report should be given the go-ahead at once.

"Whatever reservations there may be on points of detail, it is vital in view of the imminence of the marching season that its key recommendations should be implemented without delay," Spring said in a statement.

Britain asked a three-man team, headed by leading academic Peter North, to propose new machinery for handling controversial parades after the province was gripped by sectarian violence last summer after Protestant marches in Catholic districts.
"I am very disappointed indeed," said Donaldson, accusing the report group of ignoring Protestant views. "This is a protesters' charter," he told Reuters.

"I don't think it will defuse the situation. In many respects it will encourage people to disrupt parades, to object to parades, and I don't see how that can bring about a resolution of the problem," said Donaldson, who is also politician in the influential Ulster Unionist Party.
But the proposal that a powerful watchdog should have responsiblity for in effect banning contentious parades got a cautious welcome in the Irish Catholic minority.

"I welcome the fact that the (report) recognises very clearly the need for accommodation and dialogue," said Brid Rodgers of the nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party. "But we would have very grave reservations about the idea put forward that the police would have residual powers to change the decision of a commission."
The Independent Review of Parades and Marches said a five-member "parades commission," rather than the police, should decide whether marches near Catholic areas should in effect be banned.
But the largely Protestant police would have the right of appeal if they believed public order was endangered.
The report was published on the 25th anniversary of Bloody Sunday when 13 Catholics on a civil rights march were shot dead by British troops in Londonderry.

The commission said the Royal Ulster Constabulary would be empowered to appeal to the government against a commission decision and the final say about preserving order should rest with the police, the report said.

Protestants deny Catholic charges of bigotry and say their annual marches show their loyalty to their faith and the British Crown. Catholics regard them as triumphalist commemorations of 300-year-old victories over the native Irish.

Two people were killed and many injured during a summer frenzy of sectarian violence in 1996. This was followed by arson attacks on churches and boycotts of Catholic and Protestant traders in some rural communities.
